aboutAuthor: Sandeep Shenoy and Dalgin Tito are investors and educators who bridge MBA theory and household reality, teaching personal finance as cycle, risk, and behavior not just valuation.

points.heading: Two perspectives, one cycle
points.body: Corporate finance tools like WACC must translate into household cycle of earn-save-invest-protect. Mapping each rupee to a stage prevents speculation masquerading as investing.

points.heading: Wealth is what you don't see
points.body: Savings rate times time beats income display. Ego tax on cars and clubs destroys compounding more than market falls do.

points.heading: Crossed-box and hand of risk
points.body: Income minus Savings equals Expenses pre-committed via auto SIP builds surplus by default. Full risk register includes job and health alongside market drawdown, with transfer via insurance.

points.heading: Room for error plus tide of time
points.body: Stress-test returns minus three percent and keep leverage low so 15-year horizon narrows variance and prevents forced sale at bottoms.

points.heading: Cycles not pigeon pecks
points.body: Twenty percent falls eight times since 1990 but recover in two years. Rebalance 50-30 on earnings yield regime rather than react to each point move.

points.heading: Percent not points, skill not luck
points.body: 500 points is 0.8 percent today. Attribute performance over ten years and ask would you repeat decision if outcome hidden to separate skill from luck.

insights: Crossed-box equation where paying yourself first after salary doubles 14-year wealth versus saving residual.
Room for error sensitivity where 12 percent assumption versus 9 percent shortfall is forty-five percent terminal wealth.
Pigeon investing neologism for pecking at budget and rate news that causes Dalbar gap of 3.9 versus 9.6 percent.
conclusion: What My MBA Did Not Teach Me moves finance from CAPM to household — aligning family risk contracts, crossed-box saving, room for error, and cycle-aware allocation so behavior not markets determines wealth.
